clinicalScope: Parasitic infections (protozoa and helminths) presenting in patients of all ages in East African low‑resource hospitals
title: Parasitic Infections in East Africa
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Parasites are organisms that live on or inside humans, causing a range of illnesses from fever to chronic gut problems. In East Africa, the most common are malaria parasites, intestinal protozoa, and soil‑transmitted helminths, each with distinct ways of spreading, diagnosing, and treating.

sections.p: Parasites encountered in East Africa fall into two major groups: protozoa (single‑celled organisms) and helminths (multicellular worms). They differ in life‑cycle complexity, transmission routes, and typical clinical syndromes.
b: Protozoa: Plasmodium spp., Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium spp., Trypanosoma brucei, Leishmania spp., Toxoplasma gondii, Strongyloides stercoralis (also a helminth but has a protozoan‑like autoinfection cycle).
Helminths: Soil‑transmitted nematodes (Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, hookworms), Schistosoma mansoni & S. haematobium, filarial worms (Wuchereria bancrofti, Loa loa).
Geographic focus: high transmission in rural, irrigated, and peri‑urban areas with limited sanitation and vector control.
Risk groups: children, pregnant women, HIV‑positive patients, and people living in poverty.

sections.p: Understanding parasite form helps recognise them on microscopy and guides treatment choices.
b: Plasmodium falciparum: ring forms, appliqué forms, multiple parasites per erythrocyte, banana‑shaped gametocytes.
Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite: single nucleus with central karyosome, ingested RBCs.
Giardia trophozoite: pear‑shaped, two nuclei, flagella, ‘face‑to‑face’ appearance.
Schistosome adult: cylindrical, tegumented, male with gynecophoric canal, female resides within.
Hookworm larva (filariform): slender, curved, capable of skin penetration.

sections.p: Parasites use specialised molecules to invade, evade immunity, and cause tissue damage.
b: Plasmodium falciparum PfEMP1: mediates cytoadherence to endothelium, causing severe malaria.
Entamoeba histolytica Gal/GalNAc lectin: adheres to colonic epithelium and triggers cytolysis.
Giardia variant‑specific surface proteins (VSPs): antigenic variation to avoid antibodies.
Schistosome cercarial elastase: degrades skin collagen for penetration.
Hookworm anticoagulant proteins: prevent clotting during blood feeding.

sections.p: Routes of acquisition reflect parasite life cycles and local environmental conditions.
b: Mosquito bite (Anopheles) → Plasmodium spp.; seasonal peaks after rains.
Contaminated water/food → Giardia, Entamoeba, Cryptosporidium; outbreaks in schools.
Skin contact with freshwater → Schistosome cercariae; common near lakes and irrigation canals.
Soil‑oral ingestion of eggs/larvae → Ascaris, Trichuris, hookworm; linked to poor sanitation.
Tsetse fly bite → Trypanosoma brucei (human African trypanosomiasis); focal in savannah zones.

sections.p: Parasite damage results from direct tissue invasion, toxin release, and immune‑mediated injury.
b: Intra‑erythrocytic replication of Plasmodium leads to hemolysis, anemia, and microvascular obstruction.
Entamoeba trophozoites secrete proteases causing colonic ulceration and liver abscesses.
Schistosome eggs lodge in portal venules, provoking granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis.
Helminth chronic infection drives eosinophilia and Th2‑type immune response, impairing vaccine efficacy.
Strongyloides autoinfection can cause hyperinfection syndrome in immunosuppressed hosts.

sections.p: Presentations range from acute febrile illness to chronic malnutrition, depending on the organism and host factors.
b: Severe malaria: fever, rigors, altered consciousness, respiratory distress, jaundice, >5% parasitemia.
Amoebic dysentery: bloody stools, abdominal cramps, possible liver abscess.
Giardiasis: watery diarrhoea, malabsorption, weight loss, especially in children.
Schistosomiasis (intestinal): abdominal pain, diarrhoea, blood in stool; (urogenital): hematuria, dysuria.
Hookworm infection: iron‑deficiency anemia, pruritic rash at entry site.

sections.p: Tests must be selected for availability; interpretation guides urgency of treatment.

sections.p: Therapy combines parasite‑specific drugs with supportive care; drug choice reflects severity, species, and resource constraints.
b: Severe malaria: intravenous artesunate (preferred over quinine) – rapid parasite clearance, lower hypoglycaemia risk.
Uncomplicated malaria: oral artemisinin‑based combination therapy (ACT) – partner drug prevents resistance.
Amoebic dysentery: metronidazole 5‑10 days followed by a luminal agent (paromomycin).
Giardiasis: metronidazole 5‑7 days; tinidazole if vomiting precludes metronidazole.
Strongyloides hyperinfection: ivermectin 200 µg/kg daily for at least 2 weeks; longer if immunosuppressed.

sections.p: Drug resistance threatens control programmes; awareness guides empiric choices.
b: Artemisinin resistance: delayed parasite clearance, especially in eastern Africa; monitor parasite clearance time (>48 h) as warning.
Sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine resistance: high prevalence; no longer first‑line for malaria prophylaxis.
Metronidazole resistance in Giardia: rare but reported; consider tinidazole or nitazoxanide if treatment fails.
Praziquantel tolerance: occasional reduced efficacy in heavy Schistosoma infections; repeat dosing may be needed.

sections.p: Control relies on vector management, sanitation, health education, and chemoprophylaxis where feasible.
b: Insecticide‑treated nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying reduce malaria transmission.
Mass drug administration (MDA) with praziquantel for schistosomiasis in endemic districts.
School‑based deworming with albendazole or mebendazole every 6‑12 months.
Safe water supply, latrine construction, and hand‑washing to curb Giardia and Entamoeba.
Travel prophylaxis with atovaquone‑proguanil or doxycycline for non‑immune visitors to high‑risk zones.

sections.p: Untreated or delayed treatment can lead to organ damage and death.
b: Cerebral malaria: seizures, coma, high mortality; requires ICU and artesunate.
Severe anemia (<5 g/dL) from malaria or hookworm → transfusion need.
Intestinal perforation or toxic megacolon in severe amoebiasis.
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis → portal hypertension, variceal bleeding.
Strongyloides hyperinfection → disseminated bacterial sepsis, especially in steroids.

sections.p: Examiners test integration of history, exam, investigations, and management under resource limits.
b: Always ask about travel, water source, vector exposure, and HIV status.
Look for fever pattern, splenomegaly, jaundice (malaria) versus chronic diarrhoea, weight loss (giardiasis), hematuria (schistosomiasis).
Prioritise rapid malaria test in any febrile patient with rigors; treat before confirm if danger signs present.
When microscopy unavailable, use RDTs or clinical algorithms; document uncertainty.
In immunocompromised hosts, broaden differential to include opportunistic parasites (Strongyloides, Toxoplasma).

whenToSeekHelp: Fever with rigors and any danger sign (altered consciousness, respiratory distress, severe anemia) – suspect severe malaria.
Acute onset of neurological deficits with malaria exposure – possible cerebral malaria.
Persistent vomiting preventing oral drug absorption in malaria or giardiasis.
Sudden massive hematuria with known schistosomiasis – risk of urinary tract obstruction.

faq.q: Why is artesunate preferred over quinine for severe malaria?
faq.a: Artesunate clears parasites faster, has fewer cardiac and hypoglycaemic side‑effects, and improves survival.

faq.q: Can a negative malaria RDT rule out malaria?
faq.a: No; false‑negatives occur with low parasitemia or HRP2 gene deletions, so repeat microscopy if suspicion remains.

faq.q: When should I give ivermectin for Strongyloides?
faq.a: In any patient with immunosuppression, corticosteroid use, or signs of hyperinfection (e.g., diffuse rash, sepsis).

exam: A 7‑year‑old presents with intermittent fever, splenomegaly, and a peripheral smear showing ring forms in 3% of RBCs – what is the next immediate step? — Start oral ACT after confirming species; no IV artesunate needed because parasitemia <5% and no danger signs.

A pregnant woman in her second trimester reports watery diarrhoea and weight loss; stool microscopy is negative. Which test is most useful and why? — Perform a Giardia antigen test because microscopy sensitivity is low and treatment (metronidazole) is safe in pregnancy after first trimester.

A patient with HIV (CD4 80) has eosinophilia and diffuse abdominal pain; stool exams are unrevealing. What parasite should you suspect and how to confirm? — Strongyloides stercoralis; order serology or PCR, and start ivermectin empirically if testing unavailable.

A febrile adult from a malaria‑endemic area has a negative malaria RDT but high clinical suspicion. What is your management? — Obtain thick/thin smear; if unavailable, treat empirically with ACT while arranging referral for microscopy.

During a malaria outbreak, a patient develops severe anemia (Hb 4 g/dL) and respiratory distress. Which complication is most likely and how to manage? — Severe malaria with metabolic acidosis; give IV artesunate, correct anemia with transfusion, and monitor in ICU.

A traveler returns with a painless ulcer on the genitalia and later develops fever and lymphadenopathy. Which parasite is responsible and what is the treatment? — Treponema pallidum is not a parasite; the correct answer is that this presentation is not a parasitic infection – differentiate from chancroid or LGV.

A school‑aged child has growth retardation, mild anemia, and a positive stool exam for Ascaris eggs. What public‑health measure will most reduce prevalence? — School‑based deworming with albendazole every 6 months combined with improved sanitation.

In a resource‑limited clinic, you cannot perform a urine filtration for Schistosoma. What clinical clue can guide presumptive treatment? — Microscopic hematuria (dipstick positive) plus exposure to freshwater bodies in endemic area warrants praziquantel.

A patient on chronic steroids develops disseminated rash, fever, and Gram‑negative bacteremia. Which parasite is likely driving this picture? — Strongyloides hyperinfection; steroids accelerate autoinfection leading to bacterial translocation.
